Issued at 244 AM CDT Wed Oct 28 2026

Early this morning water vapor satellite imagery along with upper 
air analysis showed an upper level trough lifting northeast across 
the northern Plains into south central Canada. A second upper level 
trough was digging southeast along the Pacific Northwest coastline. 
A broad upper level ridge was located across the southeast US.

the 6Z surface map showed a lee surface low over southeast CO, with 
a surface warm front extending northeast across northwest KS, then 
northeast into western IA. Temperatures south of the warm front 
across the CWA were in the lower to mid 60s.


Today through Thursday night:

Early this morning a 40 KT LLJ may cause some isolated showers to 
develop across the eastern half of the CWA. Most CAMs show isolated 
showers developing across the eastern half of the CWA. The PBL will 
mix deep enough by the mid and late morning hours to bring an end 
to the isentropic lift showers. Skies may clear by afternoon. As the 
lee low deepens in eastern CO, southerly winds will increase late 
this morning and through the afternoon hours, with winds of 15 to 
25 MPH and gust of 25 to 35 MPH.

The H5 trough across the Pacific Northwest will shift east across 
the northern Plains and into the upper Midwest by Thursday night. 
The low-level CAA across the northern and central Plains will cause 
the boundary across NE to shift southeast across the CWA. There will 
be enough convergence along the front for scattered showers and 
thunderstorms to back build from southwest IA/southeast NE into 
northwest KS during the evening hours. MLCAPES will be in the 1000 to 
1500 J/KG range, so there should be some thunderstorms. However, 
effective shear will only be 20-25 KTS. Therefore, these storms 
should not be severe.

The NAM12, RAP, GFS, and RAP show the front stalling out along or 
just south of I-70 early Thursday morning. This will continue the 
chances for showers and thunderstorms across much of the area 
Thursday into Thursday night.

Highs Today will warm to around 80 degrees with most areas seeing 
isolation during the afternoon hours. Highs on Thursday will only 
reach the mid 70s north of the front, with highs around 80 south of 
the front.

Friday through Wednesday:

The extended range models are in good agreement showing longer wave-
length upper trough developing across the western US. The 
southwesterly flow across the central conus will cause a couple of 
southern stream H5 troughs to lift northeast across western TX into 
eastern KS Friday night. As the H5 trough approaches, DCVA ahead of 
the H5 trough will increase ascent and the boundary south of I-70 
will lift northward into central NE. Expect periods of showers and 
scattered thunderstorms to develop Friday and continue into Saturday 
morning. The thunderstorms should shift northeast of the area during
the morning hours, and there could be a break in the rain Saturday 
evening (Halloween). But the southerly transport of moisture into 
eastern KS may cause showers to continue into Saturday night. The 
cloud cover and chances for rain will keep highs slightly cooler on 
Friday, with highs in the 70s. Highs will only reach the upper 60s 
to lower 70s on Saturday.

The northern stream and southern stream H5 troughs across the western
US will phase together across the southwest US. On Sunday, expect 
only isolated to scattered showers due to isentropic lift as the 
southern stream H5 trough will fill as it shifts east of the area.

As the southern stream and northern stream H5 troughs phase together, 
they will amplify into a deep H5 low across NM by Tuesday. A 60 to 
70 KT jet max will will lift northeast across KS on Monday. A deep 
surface low across eastern CO will move northeast into south central 
NE by 00Z TUE. If there was good instability ahead of the front 
moving east across central KS, there would be a potential severe 
weather outbreak. However, cloud cover and periods of showers and 
thunderstorms may prevent sufficient instability from developing for 
widespread severe weather. However,, given 50 to 60 KT southerly 
850mb winds Monday afternoon and a line of storms that develops along
the surface front, this line of storms can tap into the stronger 
winds aloft and may produce damaging wind gusts monday afternoon. We 
will have to watch the potential for severe thunderstorms Monday 
afternoon with such a dynamic system. The transport of rich gulf 
moisture northward may provide for periods of heavy rainfall Sunday 
night through Monday night. NBM shows 1.5" to 2.5" of rainfall Friday
through Tuesday.

Both the GFS and ECMWF track the deep H5 low east across northern 
OK on Tuesday. The thunderstorms and richer moisture will pivot 
northeast of the area Monday night but expect rain to continue as 
frontogenesis develops north of the H5 low track. The periods of 
rain will continue into Wednesday before the upper low shifts east 
into western AR.
